Specification: **Err1** — *identifying errors in purported proofs*; **Err2** — *being aware of common
mathematical errors in purported proofs, for example claiming "if $ab=ac$, then $b=c$" or assuming "if
$\sin A=\sin B$, then $A=B$", neither of which are valid deductions.*
Official source: **Notes on Logic and Proof**, pp. 72–74.

::: {.callout-important}
## Why this shows up on TMUA

Paper 2 gives you a proof that **looks completely convincing** and asks: *"which line contains the
error?"* (Err1), or it tests whether you recognise a **classic invalid deduction** (Err2). Every line can
be individually true and the argument still be wrong — the flaw is a step that **does not follow**, or one
that is **only valid in a case the proof forgot to rule out**. You are not checking arithmetic; you are
checking *logic*.
:::

<div class="fs-sub">A purported proof is presented; one step is invalid. Read it line by line and ask of each step: "is this true for <em>every</em> case the line above allows?" The error is almost always a hidden division by zero, a lost sign, or an implication used backwards.</div>

## The catalogue — where proofs break

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Dividing by zero

The most common trap. Cancelling a factor $(a-b)$ is only legal when $a-b\neq0$ — but in a "$1=2$" proof,
that factor **is** zero.

$$ab=ac \;\not\Rightarrow\; b=c \quad(\text{false when }a=0)$$

[if a line divides by an expression, check it can't be $0$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Squaring and rooting

Squaring both sides can **add** solutions; taking a square root **loses the $\pm$**.

$$x^2=9\;\Rightarrow\;x=\pm3,\ \text{not just }3$$

[$\sqrt x=x-2$ squared gives $x=1$ or $4$; only $x=4$ works]{.eg}

Squaring is therefore safe as a **necessary-condition** step:
$A=B\Rightarrow A^2=B^2$. It is not automatically an **equivalence**. You may write “any solution must
satisfy the squared equation”, but not “this is equivalent to the squared equation” unless the signs make
the reverse implication valid (for example, both sides are known to be non-negative).
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Implication used backwards

Assuming $B\Rightarrow A$ because $A\Rightarrow B$ is true. The converse is a **different** statement.

$$A\Rightarrow B \;\text{ does not give }\; B\Rightarrow A$$

[proving "if it rained the ground is wet" then concluding rain from wet ground]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Circular reasoning

A step that **assumes the very thing** being proved. Every line may be true, yet nothing is established.

[a "proof" of $\sqrt2$ irrational that uses "$\sqrt2$ is irrational" partway]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Non-injective functions

*Non-injective* means **not one-to-one**: two different inputs can share one output, so equal outputs need
not mean equal inputs. Spot it with the **horizontal line test** — if any horizontal line meets the graph
more than once, the function is not one-to-one. $\sin$, $\cos$, $x^2$, $|x|$ all fail it.

$$\sin A=\sin B\;\not\Rightarrow\;A=B$$

[$\sin30^\circ=\sin150^\circ$ but $30\neq150$ — the line $y=\tfrac12$ cuts $y=\sin\theta$ twice]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Inequalities and signs

Multiplying an inequality by a quantity of **unknown sign** is invalid — the direction may flip.

$$\tfrac1x<2 \;\not\Rightarrow\; 1<2x \quad(\text{fails when }x<0)$$

[multiply by $x$ only after splitting into $x>0$ and $x<0$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Logs with a base below $1$

$\log_a$ with $0<a<1$ is a **decreasing** function, so taking it of both sides **reverses** the inequality —
and the argument must stay $>0$.

$$\log_a f<\log_a g \iff f>g \quad(0<a<1)$$

[$\log_{1/2}$ of $\left(\tfrac14\right)^n<\left(\tfrac1{32}\right)^{10}$ — the 2017 P2 Q18 flip (Question 18 below)]{.eg}
:::

::::

## How to read a suspect proof

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### The line-by-line test

For each step ask two questions: **(1)** “does this follow from the line above?” and **(2)** “does the
wording claim only a necessary condition ($\Rightarrow$), or full equivalence ($\Leftrightarrow$)?” The first
false *claim* is the error. A true one-way implication is not itself an error; treating it as reversible is.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The usual suspects, in order

Scan for: **(1)** a division/cancel — is it ever $0$? **(2)** a square root or a squaring — lost sign or
gained root? **(3)** a converse used as if proved. **(4)** the conclusion sneaking into a premise.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Where it shows up (cross-exam)

Err1/Err2 on Paper 2; the same "find the flaw" skill appears in **MAT/STEP** "explain why this argument is
wrong" parts and in the classic fake "$1=2$" proofs.
:::

::::

:::::

## Notes

### The method: test every step against every case

A suspect proof is designed to look right. Do not read it for *plausibility*: read it for *validity*, one
step at a time.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Method

**1.** Take each line and ask **"does it follow from the line above, for every value allowed so far?"**

**2.** Watch the four hotspots: a **cancel/division** (could it be $0$?), a **square/root** (lost sign or
gained root?), a **converse** (was it actually proved?), the **conclusion** (did it sneak into a premise?).

**3.** The **first** line that fails is the answer. Errors after it do not matter, and a chain can contain
two bad steps.

**Where the blame goes.** A non-reversible step is not automatically wrong: it can be a valid
**necessary-condition** step. The error is the first **false claim**. If line 2 says "equivalent" when
squaring is only one-way, line 2 is wrong; if it says "any solution must satisfy", line 2 is valid and the
error may be the later line that calls unchecked candidates "solutions". See
**[S7 Extended](s07_extended_equivalence.qmd)** for the full rule, which is the single most common source
of a wrong answer on this question type.
:::

The classic illustration is the "proof" that $2=1$. Let $a=b$. Then $a^2=ab$, so $a^2-b^2=ab-b^2$, which
factorises to $(a-b)(a+b)=b(a-b)$. Dividing by $(a-b)$ gives $a+b=b$, and since $a=b$ this says $2b=b$, so
$2=1$. Every line up to the factorisation is valid. The break is the cancel: since $a=b$, the factor $a-b$
is $0$, so that step divides by zero. *The tell: a cancel of a factor that an earlier line has forced to be
$0$.*

### The safe move for each trap

Every classic error has a matching **error-free technique**. Spotting the flaw and knowing the right way to
do it are two halves of the same skill, and the solutions below give both.

| The trap | The safe move | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Dividing by a variable (loses a root) | Move everything to one side and **factor** — never divide by something that could be $0$. | $x^2=5x\Rightarrow x(x-5)=0\Rightarrow x=0$ or $5$ |
| Square-rooting (loses the $\pm$) | Write $\sqrt{x^2}=\lvert x\rvert$, so keep **both** signs. | $x^2=9\Rightarrow x=\pm3$ |
| Squaring an equation (may add roots) | Either retain the sign condition to preserve **equivalence**, or use the squared equation only as a **necessary condition**, call its roots candidates, and check them in the original. | $\sqrt{2x+3}=x\Rightarrow 2x+3=x^2$; candidates $3,-1$, but only $3$ works |
| A trig equation "solved" once | Find the principal value, then **sketch the graph** and read off *all* solutions in the interval. | $\sin\theta=\tfrac12\Rightarrow \theta=30^\circ,\,150^\circ$ |
| Multiplying/dividing an inequality | If the multiplier's sign is unknown, **split into cases** (or multiply by a square, which is $\ge0$); by a negative, **flip** the sign. | $\dfrac1x<2\Rightarrow x<0$ or $x>\tfrac12$ |
| Using the converse | Use an implication **only in its stated direction**; test the actual claim directly. | $x>2\Rightarrow x^2>4$, but **not** the reverse ($x=-3$) |
| Assuming what you're proving | Reach the conclusion from the assumption — **never state it as a reason**. | a "$\sqrt2$ irrational" proof that cites "$\sqrt2$ is irrational" |

### The horizontal line test — seeing "not one-to-one"

The reason $\sin A=\sin B$ does not force $A=B$ is that $\sin$ is **not one-to-one**. A quick visual check:
draw any **horizontal line** $y=c$; if it meets the graph **more than once**, two different inputs give the
same output, so the function is not one-to-one. Below, one horizontal line meets each graph **twice** —
those two crossings are exactly the two solutions a naive "take the inverse once" would miss.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.4, 6.6))

# sin on [0,360]: y = 1/2 crosses at 30 and 150
t = np.linspace(0, 360, 800)
ax1.plot(t, np.sin(np.radians(t)), lw=2)
ax1.axhline(0.5, color='crimson', lw=1.6, ls='--')
for x in (30, 150):
    ax1.plot(x, 0.5, 'o', color='crimson', ms=7)
    ax1.annotate(f'{x}°', (x, 0.5), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(0, 10),
                 ha='center', color='crimson', fontsize=11)
ax1.set_title(r'$y=\sin\theta$ meets $y=\frac{1}{2}$ twice  →  $\theta=30°$ and $150°$', fontsize=12)
ax1.set_xlim(0, 360); ax1.set_xticks(range(0, 361, 90))
ax1.set_ylim(-1.2, 1.4); ax1.axhline(0, color='0.6', lw=0.8); ax1.grid(alpha=0.25)

# x^2: y = 4 crosses at x = -2 and 2
x = np.linspace(-3.2, 3.2, 400)
ax2.plot(x, x**2, lw=2)
ax2.axhline(4, color='crimson', lw=1.6, ls='--')
for xv in (-2, 2):
    ax2.plot(xv, 4, 'o', color='crimson', ms=7)
    ax2.annotate(f'x={xv}', (xv, 4), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(0, 10),
                 ha='center', color='crimson', fontsize=11)
ax2.set_title(r'$y=x^2$ meets $y=4$ twice  →  $x=-2$ and $2$', fontsize=12)
ax2.set_xlim(-3.2, 3.2); ax2.set_ylim(0, 10.5)
ax2.axvline(0, color='0.6', lw=0.8); ax2.grid(alpha=0.25)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Whenever a step "cancels" such a function — writing $A=B$ from $\sin A=\sin B$, or $x=3$ from $x^2=9$ — the
horizontal line test is the warning sign that a second solution has been dropped.

### Extraneous solutions — the squaring trap

The key is to read each step as one of two kinds of arrow:

- $\Rightarrow$ (**one-way** — "this follows"): the next line is true whenever this one is, but *not*
  necessarily the reverse. Squaring is one-way: $x=y\Rightarrow x^2=y^2$, but $x^2=y^2$ does **not** give
  $x=y$ (take $x=-3,\,y=3$).
- $\Leftrightarrow$ (**two-way** — "same solutions"): each line has exactly the same solution set as the
  last. Rearranging and factoring are two-way.

A one-way step can *enlarge* the solution set — it may drag in values that never solved the original.
That is not yet a logical error if the new equation is presented only as a **necessary condition**. After
squaring, either carry the missing sign condition so that the chain remains equivalent, or **substitute
every candidate back** before calling it a solution.

Take a student who solves $\sqrt x=x-2$ by squaring: $x=(x-2)^2$, so $x^2-5x+4=0$, so $(x-1)(x-4)=0$, and
concludes "$x=1$ or $x=4$". Label each step:

- **Squaring** is *one-way*. If $\sqrt x=x-2$ then $x=(x-2)^2$ is a **true** implication, so this line
  contains no error when it is read as a necessary condition.
- **Rearranging and factorising** are *two-way*, and keep exactly the same solutions.
- **The conclusion** is the leap. The roots $1$ and $4$ are correct **for the quadratic**, but after a
  one-way step they are only **candidates** for the original equation.

Substitute back: $x=4$ gives $\sqrt4=2=4-2$ ✓, while $x=1$ gives $\sqrt1=1$ but $1-2=-1$ ✗. So only $x=4$
solves the original. *Whenever a proof squares both sides, ask which route it is taking: preserve equivalence
with sign conditions, or deliberately move to a necessary condition and check the candidates later.*

### Log inequalities when the base is a fraction

[Question 18](#question-18-2017-p2-q18) (2017 P2 Q18) hides a sign flip inside a logarithm: the student takes $\log_{1/2}$ of both
sides of $\left(\tfrac14\right)^n<\left(\tfrac1{32}\right)^{10}$ and *keeps* the "$<$". The reason it breaks
is the **base**. A logarithm $\log_a x$ is **increasing** when $a>1$ but **decreasing** when $0<a<1$: with a
fractional base, as $x$ grows the output *falls*, because $\log_{1/a}x=-\log_a x$: the curve is the
$a>1$ curve reflected in the $x$-axis.

Put the two bases side by side and solve the **same** inequality on each. The shaded answers come out
pointing in opposite directions, and only the fractional-base one needs the domain patched on.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "The same inequality, log_a x > 2, solved on each side. With a>1 the answer is the unbounded ray x>4. With 0<a<1 the order flips, so the answer is bounded above — and the domain x>0 becomes the other half of it."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

INC, DEC, LINE, SH = '#1f77b4', '#2ca02c', '#d62728', '#7a5195'
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 4.6))
x = np.linspace(0.015, 8, 1200)

def panel(ax, base, colour, title, cross, shade, answer, verdict):
    ax.plot(x, np.log(x) / np.log(base), color=colour, lw=2.6)
    ax.axhline(2, color=LINE, ls=':', lw=1.5)
    ax.text(7.8, 2.3, '$y=2$', color=LINE, fontsize=10, ha='right')
    ax.axvspan(shade[0], shade[1], color=SH, alpha=0.16)
    ax.plot(shade, [0, 0], color=SH, lw=7, solid_capstyle='butt', zorder=4)
    ax.plot([cross], [2], 'o', color=colour, ms=8, zorder=5)
    ax.annotate('crosses $y=2$\nat $x=%s$' % ('4' if base > 1 else '0.25'), (cross, 2),
                textcoords='offset points', xytext=(-128, -84) if base > 1 else (96, -34),
                fontsize=10, color=colour,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=colour, lw=1.2))
    ax.annotate(answer, (min(shade[1], 6.0) if base > 1 else 0.13, 0),
                textcoords='offset points', xytext=(0, -54), ha='center',
                fontsize=11, color=SH,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=SH, lw=1.3))
    ax.axhline(0, color='0.7', lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0, color='0.55', lw=1.1)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.7, 8); ax.set_ylim(-4.2, 4.2)
    ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11.5)
    ax.text(0.5, -0.34, verdict, transform=ax.transAxes, ha='center', fontsize=11, color=colour)
    ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)

panel(axes[0], 2, INC, 'base $a>1$:   $y=\\log_2 x$   INCREASING',
      4, (4, 8), '$x>4$', 'order KEPT:  $\\log_2 x>2$  gives  $x>4$')
panel(axes[1], 0.5, DEC, 'base $0<a<1$:   $y=\\log_{1/2} x$   DECREASING',
      0.25, (0.0, 0.25), '$0<x<0.25$', 'order FLIPPED:  $\\log_{1/2}x>2$  gives  $0<x<0.25$')

plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0.09, 1, 1]); plt.show()
```

Two things must happen every time, and Err2 is built on forgetting either one.

::: {.keyline}
**1. Flip the sign.** For $0<a<1$, dropping the log **reverses** the inequality:
$$\log_a f(x)<\log_a g(x)\iff f(x)>g(x),\qquad \log_a f(x)<b\iff f(x)>a^{b}.$$
&nbsp; **2. Keep the argument positive.** A logarithm only exists for a positive argument, so **intersect**
with $f(x)>0$. When the flip produces an *upper* bound, the "$>0$" **lower** bound is the easy thing to lose.
:::

Two illustrations of both moves together:

- $\log_{0.5}x>2$. The base is below $1$, so removing the log reverses the "$>$": $x<0.5^{2}=0.25$. The
  domain needs $x>0$, so the answer is $0<x<0.25$. *Writing only "$x<0.25$" is the trap: it wrongly admits
  $x=-1$, where $\log_{0.5}x$ is not even defined.*
- $\log_{1/3}(x-1)>1$. Flip: $x-1<\tfrac13$, so $x<\tfrac43$. The domain needs $x-1>0$, so $x>1$. The answer
  is $1<x<\tfrac43$.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Core checklist — a log inequality with base $<1$**

- Did you **reverse** the inequality direction when you removed the log?
- Did you **intersect** with the condition that **every argument is $>0$**?
:::

# Part 1 — Concept checks

## Question 1

::: {.question}
A student solves $x^2=5x$. Which line contains the first error?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** $x^2=5x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** Divide both sides by $x$: $\;x=5$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** So the only solution is $x=5$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** line (1) &nbsp; **B** line (2) &nbsp; **C** line (3) &nbsp; **D** the argument is valid
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Dividing by a variable)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**B.** Dividing by $x$ assumes $x\neq0$, but $x=0$ **is** a solution ($0^2=5\cdot0$). Line (2) throws it
away. The full solution is $x=0$ or $x=5$. $\;\blacksquare$

**Do it right.** Never divide by a variable. Move everything to one side and **factor**:
$x^2-5x=0\Rightarrow x(x-5)=0\Rightarrow x=0$ or $x=5$. Factoring keeps the root that dividing would
delete.
:::

:::

## Question 2

::: {.question}
Which line contains the first error?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** $x^2=16$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** Take the square root: $\;x=4$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** So $x=4$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** line (1) &nbsp; **B** line (2) &nbsp; **C** line (3) &nbsp; **D** the argument is valid
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Lost sign)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**B.** $\sqrt{x^2}=|x|$, so $x^2=16$ gives $x=\pm4$. Line (2) drops the negative root $x=-4$.
$\;\blacksquare$

**Do it right.** When you square-root both sides, keep the $\pm$: $x=\pm\sqrt{16}=\pm4$. (Equivalently
factor $x^2-16=(x-4)(x+4)=0$, which shows both roots at once.)
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}

:::

# Part 2 — Medium

## Question 3

::: {.question}
Solving $\sqrt{2x+3}=x$. Which line contains the first error?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** $\sqrt{2x+3}=x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** Squaring, **this is equivalent to** $2x+3=x^2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** So $x^2-2x-3=0$, i.e. $(x-3)(x+1)=0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(4)** **The solutions are** $x=3$ and $x=-1$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** line (2) &nbsp; **B** line (3) &nbsp; **C** line (4) &nbsp; **D** the argument is valid
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Extraneous root; and the line the exam blames is not the obvious one)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**A — line (2).**

Two lines look wrong here, and **which one the exam calls the error is the whole question.**

| line | what it does | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **(2)** | claims the squared equation is **equivalent** | ✗ **the error.** Squaring is reversible **only when both sides are known to be non-negative**. The left side is; nothing so far says $x\ge0$ about the right. The two equations have **different solution sets** — $\{3\}$ against $\{3,-1\}$ — so "is equivalent to" is false. |
| **(3)** | rearranges and factorises line (2) | ✓ exact algebra |
| **(4)** | states the roots of line (3) | ✓ correct — $3$ and $-1$ **are** the roots of that quadratic |

So line (4) is where the damage becomes **visible**; in this version line (2) is where it was **done**,
because line (2) explicitly makes the false two-way claim **“equivalent”**. Without that word, the answer
would depend on whether the squared equation was introduced as a necessary condition or a replacement.

**The check anyway:** $x=3$ gives $\sqrt9=3$ ✓; $x=-1$ gives $\sqrt1=1\neq-1$ ✗. $\;\blacksquare$

**Do it right — two repairs, and they are not the same.**

1. **Keep the chain an equivalence.** Write the sign condition *before* squaring: "since $\sqrt{\;}\ge0$,
   the equation forces $x\ge0$; both sides are now non-negative, so squaring is reversible." Then no
   candidate needs checking, because none is ever gained.
2. **Accept a one-way chain, and filter at the end.** Square, solve, then **substitute every candidate into
   the original** and keep only those that fit.

Both give $x=3$. But **only the first makes line (2) legitimate** — and the exam marks the missing
justification at the line where it was needed, not at the line where the wrong answer appears.

**The word that decides it is "equivalent".** Had line (2) instead said *"any solution must satisfy
$2x+3=x^{2}$"*, that would be a **true** statement — a necessary condition is not an error — and the first
false claim would move to line (4), *"the solutions are"*. Same algebra, different answer, decided by four
English words. **[S7 Extended](s07_extended_equivalence.qmd)** works that pair side by side.

*This is [Question 10](#question-10-jz-maths-mock-b-p2-q2) (JZ Mock B P2 Q2) in miniature: identical shape, and its official
answer is the squaring step too — there the options all open with "the final answers are wrong", which
concedes the last line and asks only where the chain broke.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 4

::: {.question}
A "proof" that $\tfrac18>\tfrac14$. Which line contains the first error? (Note $\log\tfrac12<0$.)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** $3>2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** Multiply both sides by $\log\tfrac12$: $\;3\log\tfrac12>2\log\tfrac12$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** So $\log\tfrac18>\log\tfrac14$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(4)** Since $\log$ is increasing, $\tfrac18>\tfrac14$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** line (2) &nbsp; **B** line (3) &nbsp; **C** line (4) &nbsp; **D** the argument is valid
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Multiply by a negative)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**A.** $\log\tfrac12$ is **negative**, so multiplying the inequality by it must **reverse** the direction:
the correct line is $3\log\tfrac12<2\log\tfrac12$. Line (2) keeps the $>$ and everything after inherits the
error. $\;\blacksquare$

*Multiplying an inequality by a negative flips it — the single most common inequality slip.*

**Do it right.** When you multiply (or divide) an inequality by a negative quantity, **reverse** the sign.
Here $3>2$ and $\log\tfrac12<0$ give $3\log\tfrac12<2\log\tfrac12$, i.e. $\log\tfrac18<\log\tfrac14$, and so
correctly $\tfrac18<\tfrac14$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

# Part 3 — Hard

## Question 5

::: {.question}
A "proof" that in any set of numbers all are equal. Which line contains the first error?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** Base case: a set of one number — all its members are equal. True.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** Assume any set of $n$ numbers are all equal.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** Take $n+1$ numbers $a_1,\dots,a_{n+1}$; the first $n$ are all equal and the last $n$ are
all equal (by the assumption).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(4)** The two groups overlap, so all $n+1$ numbers are equal.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(5)** By induction, in any set all numbers are equal.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** line (2) &nbsp; **B** line (3) &nbsp; **C** line (4) &nbsp; **D** the argument is valid
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(The induction gap)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**C.** The overlap argument fails at the very first step, $n=1\to2$: the two groups are $\{a_1\}$ and
$\{a_2\}$, which share **no** element, so nothing forces $a_1=a_2$. Line (4) assumes an overlap that
doesn't exist when $n=1$, and the whole induction never gets off the ground. $\;\blacksquare$

*A famous fake: the inductive step must work for the smallest case it claims to cover.*

**Do it right.** Before trusting an induction, **test the step at its first instance** ($n=1\to2$). Here it
fails — two single numbers need not be equal — so the "theorem" is false. There is no fix; the statement
itself is untrue.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 6

::: {.question}
A proof that "if $n^2$ is even then $n$ is even." Which line contains the first error?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** We prove the contrapositive: if $n$ is odd then $n^2$ is odd.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** Assume $n$ is odd, so $n=2k+1$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** Then $n^2=4k^2+4k+1=2(2k^2+2k)+1$, which is odd.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(4)** So $n$ odd $\Rightarrow n^2$ odd; the contrapositive holds, hence so does the original.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** line (1) &nbsp; **B** line (2) &nbsp; **C** line (3) &nbsp; **D** the argument is valid
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Is it actually valid?)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**D.** Every step is correct: proving the contrapositive is legitimate, the algebra is right, and the
contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original. There is no error. $\;\blacksquare$

*Not every "spot the error" question has an error — sometimes the skill is recognising a sound proof.*

**Do it right.** Nothing to fix — this is the *model* of a clean contrapositive proof: state the
contrapositive, assume its hypothesis, derive its conclusion, done. Confirm each step follows and select
"valid".
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

# Part 4 — Exam bank: mock papers

Each pair below shows the **same** fallacy from two sides, so read them two at a time. **Q14** and **Q15**
are genuine past papers placed here for that reason; the rest of the real papers are in Part 5. **★** marks
a question that has already come up on a mock sat here.

---

**Questions 7–9 · Dividing — when it destroys solutions, and when it is perfectly safe.**
Cancelling a factor is only legal if that factor can never be $0$. The third question is the control: there
the factor *is* always positive, so the division is fine.

## Question 7 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set B · P2 Q4</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following attempt at finding the number of solutions to
$$6\sin x=7\tan x\qquad\text{for }0\le x\le 360.$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $6\sin x=7\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $6=\dfrac{7}{\cos x}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; $\cos x=\dfrac67$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV** &nbsp; There are two real solutions to this equation.

Which statement describes this attempt?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** completely correct &nbsp; **B** first mistake on line I &nbsp; **C** first mistake on line II
&nbsp; **D** first mistake on line III &nbsp; **E** first mistake on line IV
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Cancelling $\sin x$)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**C.** Line I is a correct rewrite of $\tan x$. Line II divides both sides by $\sin x$ — *and $\sin x=0$ is
allowed here*, so every solution with $\sin x=0$ is thrown away. Those are the **only** solutions: if
$\sin x\neq0$ then line II forces $\cos x=\tfrac76>1$, which is impossible.

*Line III is wrong too — $6=\tfrac{7}{\cos x}$ gives $\cos x=\tfrac76$, not $\tfrac67$ — but the question asks
for the **first** mistake, and that is line II.*

**Do it right.** Factorise instead of dividing:
$$6\sin x\cos x-7\sin x=0\;\Longrightarrow\;\sin x\,(6\cos x-7)=0 .$$
The bracket never vanishes, so $\sin x=0$, giving $x=0^\circ,\,180^\circ,\,360^\circ$ — **three** solutions,
not two. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 8 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock E · P2 Q2</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following attempt to solve $(x-2)\sqrt{x+3}=x^{2}-5x+6$:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(I)** &nbsp; $(x-2)\sqrt{x+3}=x^{2}-5x+6$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(II)** &nbsp; $(x-2)\sqrt{x+3}=(x-2)(x-3)$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(III)** &nbsp; $\sqrt{x+3}=x-3$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(IV)** &nbsp; $x+3=(x-3)^{2}$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(V)** &nbsp; $x+3=x^{2}-6x+9$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(VI)** &nbsp; $x^{2}-7x+6=0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(VII)** &nbsp; $(x-1)(x-6)=0$

The solutions are concluded to be $x=1$ and $x=6$. Which one of the following is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** entirely correct &nbsp; **B** first error (I)$\to$(II) &nbsp; **C** first error (II)$\to$(III)
&nbsp; **D** first error (III)$\to$(IV) &nbsp; **E** first error (IV)$\to$(V) &nbsp; **F** first error (V)$\to$(VI)
&nbsp; **G** first error (VI)$\to$(VII)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Cancelling a bracket that can vanish)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**C.** Step (I)$\to$(II) is a correct factorisation. Step (II)$\to$(III) **divides by $(x-2)$**, which is $0$
when $x=2$ — and $x=2$ *is* a solution of the original equation (both sides are $0$). It is lost.

*Two separate faults follow from that one habit.* After (III), squaring at (IV) needs $x-3\ge0$; the root
$x=1$ fails that test, so it is **spurious**. The true solution set is $x=2$ and $x=6$ — the attempt loses one
root and invents another.

**Do it right.** Move everything to one side and factor:
$(x-2)\big(\sqrt{x+3}-(x-3)\big)=0$, then solve the two factors **separately**, checking $x-3\ge0$ on the
second. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 9 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock C · P2 Q6</span>

::: {.question}
Let $x\neq0$ and $f(x)=\tfrac37x^{7/3}+\tfrac34x^{4/3}-6x^{1/3}$. A student finds the values of $x$ for which
the curve is increasing:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $f'(x)=x^{4/3}+x^{1/3}-2x^{-2/3}$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $f'(x)=x^{-2/3}\left(x^{2}+x-2\right)$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; $x^{-2/3}\left(x^{2}+x-2\right)\ge0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV** &nbsp; $x^{2}+x-2\ge0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**V** &nbsp; $(x-1)(x+2)\ge0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VI** &nbsp; $x\le-2$ or $x\ge1$

Which of the following is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** first error step I &nbsp; **B** step II &nbsp; **C** step III &nbsp; **D** step IV &nbsp;
**E** step V &nbsp; **F** step VI &nbsp; **G** the student's answer is correct
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(The division that **is** allowed)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**G — there is no error.** Run the checklist and every step survives:

- **I.** $\tfrac37\cdot\tfrac73=1$, $\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac43=1$, $6\cdot\tfrac13=2$, so
  $f'(x)=x^{4/3}+x^{1/3}-2x^{-2/3}$. ✓
- **II.** $x^{4/3}=x^{-2/3}\!\cdot\!x^{2}$ and $x^{1/3}=x^{-2/3}\!\cdot\!x$, so the factorisation is exact. ✓
- **III.** Increasing means $f'(x)\ge0$. ✓
- **IV.** *This is the step the question is really testing.* Dividing by $x^{-2/3}$ is legal precisely because
  $x^{-2/3}=\dfrac{1}{\left(x^{1/3}\right)^{2}}>0$ **for every** $x\neq0$ — a positive divisor, so the
  inequality keeps its direction. ✓
- **V, VI.** $x^{2}+x-2=(x-1)(x+2)$, positive outside the roots. ✓

**Compare with Q7 and Q8.** All three divide by something. Here the divisor is provably positive, so
nothing is lost; there the divisor could be $0$, so solutions vanished. *The test is never "did they divide?"
— it is "**can the divisor be zero?**" .* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

**Questions 10–12 · Squaring — roots gained, conditions lost, and one squaring that is fine.**
Squaring is reversible only when **both sides are known to be non-negative**. Check that before you object
to it — the last of the three is a trap for students who have learned to distrust squaring on sight.

## Question 10 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock B · P2 Q2</span>

::: {.question}
A student solves $\dfrac{\sqrt{x^{3}+x^{2}-x}+2}{x+2}=1$:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**Step (1)** &nbsp; Multiply both sides by $x+2$: $\;\sqrt{x^{3}+x^{2}-x}+2=x+2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**Step (2)** &nbsp; Subtract $2$ from both sides: $\;\sqrt{x^{3}+x^{2}-x}=x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**Step (3)** &nbsp; Square both sides: $\;x^{3}+x^{2}-x=x^{2}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**Step (4)** &nbsp; Rearrange: $\;x^{3}-x=0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**Step (5)** &nbsp; Factorise: $\;x(x-1)(x+1)=0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**Step (6)** &nbsp; Deduce $x=-1,\,0,\,1$.

Which one of the following is correct?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** answers wrong, first error Step (1) &nbsp; **B** Step (2) &nbsp; **C** Step (3) &nbsp;
**D** Step (4) &nbsp; **E** Step (5) &nbsp; **F** Step (6) &nbsp; **G** the answers are correct, no error
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Squaring invents a root)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**C.** Steps (1) and (2) are both genuine equivalences — the $+2$ sits **outside** the square root, so
subtracting it is legitimate.

Step (3) squares $\sqrt{x^{3}+x^{2}-x}=x$. A square root is never negative, so this equation silently
requires $\boxed{x\ge0}$; treating the squared equation as an **equivalent replacement** drops that
condition, and any negative solution of the squared equation is spurious.

*Check the three candidates in the line before squaring, $\sqrt{x^{3}+x^{2}-x}=x$:*

- $x=-1$: LHS $=\sqrt{-1+1+1}=1$, RHS $=-1$. **Fails** — invented by the squaring.
- $x=0$: $0=0$. ✓
- $x=1$: $\sqrt{1+1-1}=1=1$. ✓

So the solutions are $x=0$ and $x=1$. The mock's official convention treats “square both sides” as a
replacement-equation step, so its intended answer is **C, Step (3)**.

**Wording warning.** Formally, the implication
$\sqrt{x^{3}+x^{2}-x}=x\Rightarrow x^{3}+x^{2}-x=x^2$ is true. If Step (3) had said **“any solution must
satisfy”**, the first error would instead be Step (6), where the candidates are promoted to solutions
without checking. To make C unambiguous, write **“this is equivalent to”** at Step (3); to make the later
answer unambiguous, write **“possible values/candidates”** and then add a separate unchecked “the
solutions are” line.

**Do it right.** Either retain $x\ge0$ so the next equation remains equivalent, or explicitly use the
squared equation only as a necessary condition and check every candidate in the original. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 11 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock B · P2 Q8</span>

::: {.question}
The following is an attempted proof of the conjecture *if $\sin\theta>\cos\theta$ then
$\sin\theta>\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$*. Suppose $\sin\theta>\cos\theta$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(I)** &nbsp; Then $\sin\theta-\cos\theta>0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(II)** &nbsp; Squaring the positive quantity $\sin\theta-\cos\theta$ gives
$(\sin\theta-\cos\theta)^{2}>0$, i.e. $1-2\sin\theta\cos\theta>0$, so $\sin\theta\cos\theta<\tfrac12$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(III)** &nbsp; Hence $(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^{2}=1+2\sin\theta\cos\theta<2$, so
$\lvert\sin\theta+\cos\theta\rvert<\sqrt2$ and in particular $\sin\theta+\cos\theta>-\sqrt2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(IV)** &nbsp; Adding (I) and (III) gives $2\sin\theta>-\sqrt2$, so
$\sin\theta>-\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$; squaring this yields $\sin^{2}\theta>\tfrac12$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(V)** &nbsp; Since $\sin^{2}\theta>\tfrac12$ means $\lvert\sin\theta\rvert>\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$, and
$\sin\theta>-\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$ rules out $\sin\theta<-\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$, we conclude
$\sin\theta>\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** the proof is correct &nbsp; **B** first error line (I) &nbsp; **C** line (II) &nbsp;
**D** line (III) &nbsp; **E** line (IV) &nbsp; **F** line (V)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Squaring an inequality)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**E.** Lines (I)–(III) are all valid: (I) rearranges the hypothesis; (II) squares a quantity **known to be
positive**, which is legal, and uses $\sin^{2}+\cos^{2}=1$ correctly; (III) is honest algebra on
$(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^{2}$.

Line (IV) adds the two inequalities correctly to reach $\sin\theta>-\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$ — and then **squares an
inequality whose sides are not both non-negative**. *That is never valid:* $a>b$ gives $a^{2}>b^{2}$ only
when $a,b\ge0$. Here $\sin\theta=0$ satisfies $\sin\theta>-\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$ but gives
$\sin^{2}\theta=0<\tfrac12$.

**The conjecture itself is false,** which is the quickest way to know an error must exist somewhere: take
$\theta=\tfrac{5\pi}{6}$, where $\sin\theta=\tfrac12$ and $\cos\theta=-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. Then
$\sin\theta>\cos\theta$ holds, yet $\sin\theta=\tfrac12<\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$.

**Do it right.** Compare (II) with (IV) on the same page: squaring is fine in (II) because positivity was
established first, and fatal in (IV) because it was not. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 12 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock A · P2 Q3 &nbsp;★</span>

::: {.question}
A student solves the inequality $\sqrt{x-3}<x-2$:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(I)** &nbsp; Can only square-root a non-negative number, therefore $x-3\ge0\iff x\ge3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(II)** &nbsp; Squaring both sides gives $x-3<(x-2)^{2}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(III)** &nbsp; Simplifies to $0<x^{2}-5x+7$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(IV)** &nbsp; The discriminant of $x^{2}-5x+7$ is $25-28=-3<0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(V)** &nbsp; Since the leading coefficient is positive, $x^{2}-5x+7>0$ for all real $x\ge3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(VI)** &nbsp; Therefore the solution is $x\ge3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** invalid, first problematic step (I) &nbsp; **B** (II) &nbsp; **C** (III) &nbsp; **D** (IV)
&nbsp; **E** (V) &nbsp; **F** (VI) &nbsp; **G** the attempt is valid and the solution is correct
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(The squaring that **is** legal)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**G — the attempt is valid.** The trap is step (II): students who have been told "you cannot square an
inequality" reject it on sight and pick **B**.

*The real rule is conditional, not absolute.* Squaring preserves an inequality exactly when **both sides are
non-negative**, and here step (I) has already established that:

- $\sqrt{x-3}\ge0$ always, and
- $x\ge3\Rightarrow x-2\ge1>0$.

So on the domain $x\ge3$,
$$\sqrt{x-3}<x-2\iff x-3<(x-2)^{2},$$
a genuine equivalence. Steps (III)–(V) are routine, and since $x^{2}-5x+7>0$ for **every** real $x$, the
inequality holds throughout the domain: the answer $x\ge3$ is right.

**Compare with Q11.** Same operation, opposite verdict — because there the sign of the sides was never
checked, and here it was checked **first**. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

---

**Questions 13–16 · Proofs about integers.** Here the algebra is usually flawless and the error is a
*logical* leap: a property of a polynomial mistaken for a property of its values, a remainder that is not
really a remainder, a "$\ge$" that should be "$>$". Two of these are real TMUA past-paper questions.

## Question 13 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock A · P2 Q5 &nbsp;★</span>

::: {.question}
A student proves: *for every positive integer $n$, if $n^{2}+2$ is prime then $n$ is a multiple of $3$.*

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I.** Suppose $n$ is a positive integer with $n^{2}+2$ prime, but $n$ not a multiple of $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II.** Then the remainder of $n$ on division by $3$ is $1$ or $2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III.** In either case $n^{2}$ leaves remainder $1$ when divided by $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV.** Therefore $n^{2}+2$ leaves remainder $0$ when divided by $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**V.** So $3$ divides $n^{2}+2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VI.** Hence $n^{2}+2=3k$ for some integer $k$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VII.** It follows that $n^{2}+2$ is composite and not prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VIII.** This contradicts the assumption in (I) that $n^{2}+2$ is prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IX.** Therefore $n$ is a multiple of $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** completely correct &nbsp; **B** line I &nbsp; **C** line II &nbsp; **D** line III &nbsp;
**E** line IV &nbsp; **F** line V &nbsp; **G** line VI &nbsp; **H** line VII &nbsp; **I** line VIII &nbsp;
**J** line IX
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*("a multiple of 3" is not "composite")*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**H.** Lines I–VI are all correct. *Check III explicitly, since it carries the argument:* if $n=3m+1$ then
$n^{2}=9m^{2}+6m+1$, remainder $1$; if $n=3m+2$ then $n^{2}=9m^{2}+12m+4=3(3m^{2}+4m+1)+1$, remainder $1$
again. Adding $2$ gives remainder $0$, so $3$ divides $n^{2}+2$ and $n^{2}+2=3k$.

Line **VII** is the break: $3k$ is composite *only when $k>1$*. If $k=1$ then $3k=3$, which is **prime**.
And that case really occurs — at $n=1$, $n^{2}+2=3$ is prime while $n=1$ is not a multiple of $3$.

*So the single value $n=1$ both falsifies the claim and kills the proof.* The claim is true for every
$n\ge2$, and the proof is valid for every $n\ge2$ — which is exactly why the flaw is easy to miss.

**The habit.** Before accepting a line like "so it is composite", ask what the **smallest** allowed value
does. $n=1$, $k=1$, the empty case: that is where these proofs die. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 14 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2016 · P2 Q13</span>

::: {.question}
In this question $a,b,c$ are positive integers. The following is an attempted proof of the **false** statement
*if $a$ divides $bc$, then $a$ divides $b$ or $a$ divides $c$*. Which line contains the error?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**1.** The statement is equivalent to "if $a$ does not divide $b$ and $a$ does not divide $c$, then $a$ does not divide $bc$".

&nbsp;&nbsp;**2.** Suppose $a$ does not divide $b$ and $a$ does not divide $c$. Then the remainder when dividing $b$ by $a$ is $r$, where $0<r<a$, and the remainder when dividing $c$ by $a$ is $s$, where $0<s<a$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**3.** So $b=ax+r$ and $c=ay+s$ for some integers $x$ and $y$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**4.** Thus $bc=a(axy+xs+yr)+rs$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**5.** So the remainder when dividing $bc$ by $a$ is $rs$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**6.** Since $r>0$ and $s>0$, it follows that $rs>0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**7.** Hence $a$ does not divide $bc$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** Line 1 &nbsp; **B** Line 2 &nbsp; **C** Line 3 &nbsp; **D** Line 4 &nbsp; **E** Line 5
&nbsp; **F** Line 6 &nbsp; **G** Line 7
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(A remainder must be smaller than the divisor)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**E.** Lines 1–4 are sound: line 1 is a correct contrapositive, and the expansion
$bc=(ax+r)(ay+s)=a(axy+xs+yr)+rs$ is exact.

Line 5 calls $rs$ *the remainder*. *A remainder is not just "what is left over" — it must satisfy
$0\le rs<a$.* All we know is $r<a$ and $s<a$ separately, so the **product can exceed $a$**; the true remainder
is $rs$ reduced mod $a$, which may well be $0$.

**Concretely:** $a=4$, $b=2$ ($r=2$), $c=2$ ($s=2$). Then $rs=4$, but $bc=4$ and $4\div4$ leaves remainder
$\mathbf0$ — so $a$ **does** divide $bc$, exactly the opposite of line 7.

*(And the statement really is false: $a=6,\ b=2,\ c=3$ gives $bc=6$, which $6$ divides, though $6$ divides
neither $2$ nor $3$. This is why some line **must** be wrong — find the first one.)* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 15 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2022 · P2 Q7</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the claim *the difference between two consecutive positive cube numbers is always prime*, with this
attempted proof:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $(x+1)^{3}=x^{3}+3x^{2}+3x+1$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; Taking $x$ a positive integer, the difference of consecutive cubes is $(x+1)^{3}-x^{3}=3x^{2}+3x+1$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; It is impossible to factorise $3x^{2}+3x+1$ into two linear factors with integer coefficients, because its discriminant is negative.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV** &nbsp; Therefore for every positive integer value of $x$, the integer $3x^{2}+3x+1$ cannot be factorised.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**V** &nbsp; Hence the difference between two consecutive cube numbers will always be prime.

Which best describes this proof? &nbsp; **A** correct, claim true &nbsp; **B** correct, but counterexamples
exist &nbsp; **C** first error line I &nbsp; **D** line II &nbsp; **E** line III &nbsp; **F** line IV &nbsp;
**G** line V
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Irreducible polynomial $\neq$ prime values)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**F.** Line III is **true**: the *polynomial* $3x^{2}+3x+1$ has discriminant $9-12=-3<0$, so it does not split
into integer linear factors.

Line IV converts that into a claim about the **integers** $3x^{2}+3x+1$, and those are different things.
*A polynomial being irreducible says nothing about whether its values are prime.* **Counterexample:** $x=5$
gives $3(25)+15+1=91=7\times13$, i.e. $6^{3}-5^{3}=91$, which is composite.

**Why not G?** Line V follows *correctly* from line IV — if the value genuinely could never be factorised it
would indeed always be prime. The conclusion is false only because IV is, and the question asks for the
**first** bad line. *The most tempting wrong answer on this question is G, chosen by reading the conclusion
first.* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 16 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock A · P2 Q17 &nbsp;★</span>

::: {.question}
Here $n$ is an integer greater than $1$.
**Statement:** *if $n$ does not divide $k!$ for any positive integer $k$ with $k<n$, then $n$ is prime.*

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** Assume $n$ does not divide $k!$ for any positive integer $k<n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** Suppose for contradiction $n$ is composite, so $n=ab$ with $1<a\le b<n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** *Case 1:* $a<b$. Then $a$ and $b$ are distinct integers in $\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(4)** So $a$ and $b$ both appear as factors of $(n-1)!=1\cdot2\cdots(n-1)$, hence $ab=n$ divides $(n-1)!$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(5)** *Case 2:* $a=b$, so $n=a^{2}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(6)** Since $a\ge2$, the integers $a$ and $2a$ satisfy $a\ge2$ and $2a\ge4$, so they are positive integers.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(7)** Since $a\ge2$ we have $a<a^{2}=n$ and $2a<a^{2}=n$, so $a$ and $2a$ are distinct integers in $\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(8)** So $a$ and $2a$ both appear as factors of $(n-1)!$, hence $2a^{2}=2n$ divides $(n-1)!$, and in particular $n$ divides $(n-1)!$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(9)** In both cases $n$ divides $(n-1)!$, contradicting line (1). Hence $n$ is prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** first mistake line 1 &nbsp; **B** line 2 &nbsp; **C** line 3 &nbsp; **D** line 4 &nbsp;
**E** line 5 &nbsp; **F** line 6 &nbsp; **G** line 7 &nbsp; **H** the proof is valid and the statement is true
&nbsp; *(options A–G each also assert that the statement is false)*
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*("$\ge$" where the argument needs "$>$")*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**G.** Line (7) claims that $a\ge2$ gives $2a<a^{2}$. *But $2a<a^{2}$ is equivalent to $a>2$, not $a\ge2$.*
At the boundary $a=2$ the claim reads $4<4$, which is false.

**The counterexample is exactly that boundary.** Take $n=4$ (so $a=b=2$, Case 2): $1!=1$, $2!=2$, $3!=6$, and
$4$ divides none of them — the hypothesis of the statement holds — yet $4$ is not prime. **So the statement
is false**, and the proof must fail somewhere; tracing $n=4$ through it, lines (1)–(6) all hold and (7) is the
first to break.

*Note how Case 1 is genuinely fine:* when $a<b$ the two factors really are distinct and both below $n$, so
$ab=n$ divides $(n-1)!$. Only the repeated-factor case needs the extra room, and only $a=2$ fails to have it.

**The habit.** When a proof splits into cases, test the **boundary of each case** — the smallest $a$, the
equality $a=b$. That is where a case-split proof breaks. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

# Part 5 — Exam bank: real past papers

Seven more genuine TMUA papers, arranged by **the kind of thing that goes wrong** rather than by topic.
Spot-the-error is one of the two most stable slots on the test — one to three questions in every sitting
from 2016 to 2023 — and across eight years the faults fall into four families:

| family | what happens | here |
|---|---|---|
| **an algebraic slip** | a sign is dropped in ordinary manipulation | Q17 |
| **direction of an inequality** | multiplying, dividing or taking a log by something negative or decreasing | Q18 |
| **a lost sign from squaring or rooting** | $\sqrt{u^{2}}=u$ instead of $\lvert u\rvert$ | Q19, Q20 |
| **direction of the argument** | the converse proved, or a theorem used outside what it says | Q21, Q22, Q23 |

**Q14** (2016 Q13) and **Q15** (2022 Q7) above are real papers too — they sit among the mocks because each
is paired with a mock question showing the same fallacy.

[Read one line at a time and ask "does this follow for **every** value the line above allows?"]{.hl} The
last two are the hardest kind: every individual line is correct, and the argument still proves the wrong
thing.

## Question 17 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2020 · P2 Q3</span>

::: {.question}
A student makes the following claim:

> For all integers $n$, the expression $\;4\left(\dfrac{9n+1}{2}-\dfrac{3n-1}{2}\right)\;$ is divisible by $3$.

Here is the student's argument:

> $4\left(\dfrac{9n+1}{2}-\dfrac{3n-1}{2}\right)=2\left(2\left(\dfrac{9n+1}{2}-\dfrac{3n-1}{2}\right)\right)$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(I)**
>
> $=2(9n+1-3n-1)$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(II)**
>
> $=2(6n)$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(III)**
>
> $=12n$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(IV)**
>
> $=3(4n)$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(V)**
>
> which is always a multiple of $3$. &nbsp;&nbsp;**(VI)**

Which one of the following is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The argument is correct. &nbsp;&nbsp;**B** first error on line (I). &nbsp;&nbsp;**C** … (II).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** … (III). &nbsp;&nbsp;**E** … (IV). &nbsp;&nbsp;**F** … (V). &nbsp;&nbsp;**G** … (VI).
:::

Nothing subtle here — just [expand the bracket honestly, watching what the minus sign does to **both**
terms]{.hl} of the second fraction. Then check the claim itself against $n=1$ before you trust the
conclusion.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — a sign dropped inside a bracket, and a conclusion that is false as well
:::

**C — the first error is on line (II).**

### What line (II) should say

Multiplying the inner bracket by $2$ clears both denominators:

$$2\left(\frac{9n+1}{2}-\frac{3n-1}{2}\right)=(9n+1)-(3n-1)=9n+1-3n\;\mathbf{+}\;1=6n+2 .$$

The student wrote $9n+1-3n-1$, applying the minus to $3n$ but **not** to $-1$. *The subtraction is of the
whole second fraction, so both of its terms change sign.*

### What follows

$$4\left(\frac{9n+1}{2}-\frac{3n-1}{2}\right)=2(6n+2)=12n+4 .$$

And now look at the claim:

$$12n+4\equiv 0+1\equiv 1 \pmod 3 ,$$

so the expression leaves remainder $1$ on division by $3$ **for every integer $n$** — it is *never*
divisible by $3$. Values: $n=1\to16$, $n=2\to28$, $n=3\to40$, $n=4\to52$. None is a multiple of $3$.

*So the sign slip did not merely weaken the argument; it turned a statement that is always false into one
that looks always true.*

**The lesson.** [Test the claim numerically before auditing the proof]{.hl}. Here $n=1$ gives $16$ in three
seconds and tells you immediately that **some** line must be wrong — which turns a six-line hunt into a
check of the one line where an expression changes shape. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 18 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2017 · P2 Q18</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following problem:

> Solve the inequality $\;\left(\dfrac14\right)^{n}<\left(\dfrac1{32}\right)^{10}$, where $n$ is a positive
> integer.

A student produces the following argument:

> $\left(\dfrac14\right)^{n}<\left(\dfrac1{32}\right)^{10}$
>
> &nbsp;&nbsp;**(I)** $\;\log_{\frac12}\left(\dfrac14\right)^{n}<\log_{\frac12}\left(\dfrac1{32}\right)^{10}$
>
> &nbsp;&nbsp;**(II)** $\;n\log_{\frac12}\left(\dfrac14\right)<10\log_{\frac12}\left(\dfrac1{32}\right)$
>
> &nbsp;&nbsp;**(III)** $\;n<\dfrac{10\log_{\frac12}\left(\frac1{32}\right)}{\log_{\frac12}\left(\frac14\right)}$
>
> &nbsp;&nbsp;**(IV)** $\;n<\dfrac{10\times5}{2}=25$
>
> &nbsp;&nbsp;**(V)** $\;1\le n\le24$

Which step (if any) in the argument is invalid?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none — the argument is correct &nbsp;&nbsp;**B** only (I) &nbsp;&nbsp;**C** only (II)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** only (III) &nbsp;&nbsp;**E** only (IV) &nbsp;&nbsp;**F** only (V)
:::

Taking logs of an inequality is safe **only** when the log is an increasing function. [The base here is
$\tfrac12$, which is less than $1$]{.hl} — so before reading any further, decide what $\log_{1/2}$ does to
the order of two numbers.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — a logarithm to a base below $1$ reverses an inequality
:::

**B — only step (I) is invalid.**

### Why (I) fails

$\log_{1/2}$ is a **decreasing** function: raising $\tfrac12$ to a larger power gives a *smaller* number,
so the log runs backwards. Concretely

$$\tfrac14>\tfrac1{32}\qquad\text{but}\qquad \log_{\frac12}\tfrac14=2\;<\;5=\log_{\frac12}\tfrac1{32} .$$

So applying $\log_{1/2}$ to both sides must **reverse** the inequality:

$$\left(\tfrac14\right)^{n}<\left(\tfrac1{32}\right)^{10}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\log_{\frac12}\left(\tfrac14\right)^{n}\;\boldsymbol{>}\;\log_{\frac12}\left(\tfrac1{32}\right)^{10} .$$

### The later steps are all fine

| | | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **(II)** | power rule $\log a^{k}=k\log a$ | ✓ an identity |
| **(III)** | divide by $\log_{1/2}\tfrac14=2$, which is **positive** | ✓ direction preserved |
| **(IV)** | $\log_{1/2}\tfrac1{32}=5$ since $\left(\tfrac12\right)^{5}=\tfrac1{32}$; $\tfrac{10\times5}{2}=25$ | ✓ |
| **(V)** | $n<25$ with $n$ a positive integer | ✓ gives $1\le n\le24$ |

*Every line after the first is impeccable, which is what makes the question hard: the damage is done
before the algebra starts.*

### The correct answer

With the inequality the right way round, $n>25$, so the solution is $n\ge26$. Check directly in powers of
$2$:

$$\left(\tfrac14\right)^{n}=2^{-2n},\qquad\left(\tfrac1{32}\right)^{10}=2^{-50},\qquad
2^{-2n}<2^{-50}\iff-2n<-50\iff n>25 . $$

*The student's answer $1\le n\le24$ is not merely incomplete: it contains no correct value at all. The one
integer in neither set is $n=25$, where the two sides are equal.*

**The lesson.** [An inequality survives $\log_b$ unchanged only when $b>1$]{.hl}. When $0<b<1$ the order
flips, exactly as it does when you multiply by a negative number. And note the cheap safety net available
here: both sides were powers of $2$ all along, so the whole question could be done without logarithms.
$\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 19 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P2 Q5</span>

::: {.question}
On which line is the **first** error in the following argument?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** &nbsp; $\sin^{2}x+\cos^{2}x=1$ for all values of $x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** &nbsp; Therefore $\cos x=\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}x}$ for all values of $x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** &nbsp; Hence $1+\cos x=1+\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}x}$ for all values of $x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** &nbsp; Thus $(1+\cos x)^{2}=\left(1+\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}x}\right)^{2}$ for all values of $x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** &nbsp; Substituting $x=\pi$ gives $0=4$.
:::

Line **E** is plainly absurd, and that is the point: [the absurdity proves an error exists, but the
question asks where it **first** occurs]{.hl}. Work forwards from A, not backwards from E.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\sqrt{u^{2}}=\lvert u\rvert$; the square root sign is always non-negative
:::

**B.**

### Why B fails

From $\sin^{2}x+\cos^{2}x=1$ we get $\cos^{2}x=1-\sin^{2}x$, and taking the square root gives

$$\lvert\cos x\rvert=\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}x} ,$$

**not** $\cos x$. *The symbol $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$ always denotes the non-negative root, so the right-hand
side can never be negative, while $\cos x$ is negative on the whole of the second and third quadrants.*

At $x=\pi$:

$$\cos\pi=-1 \qquad\text{but}\qquad \sqrt{1-\sin^{2}\pi}=\sqrt{1-0}=+1 .$$

So line B is already false, at the very value the argument later substitutes.

### The later lines are fine

C adds $1$ to both sides of B; D squares both sides of C; E substitutes $x=\pi$. *Each of those is a valid
operation performed on a false statement — which is exactly how a false line propagates into nonsense
without any further mistake being made.* Tracking E: $\;(1+\cos\pi)^{2}=0$ and
$\left(1+\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}\pi}\right)^{2}=(1+1)^{2}=4$.

**The lesson.** [Square-rooting loses the sign, every time]{.hl}. Write $\sqrt{u^{2}}=\lvert u\rvert$ and
then decide, from the range of $x$, whether the modulus can be removed. *And when a chain ends in an
obvious absurdity, the error is almost never in the last line — it is in the first line that quietly
assumed a sign.* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 20 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2018 · P2 Q13</span>

::: {.question}
The following is an attempted proof of the conjecture:

> **if** $\tan\theta>0$, **then** $\sin\theta+\cos\theta>1$.

> Suppose $\tan\theta>0$, so in particular $\cos\theta\neq0$.
>
> &nbsp;&nbsp;**(I)** &nbsp; Since $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$, then $\sin\theta\cos\theta=\tan\theta\cos^{2}\theta>0$.
>
> &nbsp;&nbsp;**(II)** &nbsp; It follows that $1+2\sin\theta\cos\theta>1$.
>
> &nbsp;&nbsp;**(III)** &nbsp; Therefore $\sin^{2}\theta+2\sin\theta\cos\theta+\cos^{2}\theta>1$,
>
> &nbsp;&nbsp;**(IV)** &nbsp; which factorises to give $(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^{2}>1$.
>
> &nbsp;&nbsp;**(V)** &nbsp; Therefore $\sin\theta+\cos\theta>1$.

Which one of the following is the case?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The proof is correct. &nbsp;&nbsp;**B** first error in (I). &nbsp;&nbsp;**C** … (II).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** … (III). &nbsp;&nbsp;**E** … (IV). &nbsp;&nbsp;**F** … (V).
:::

The same fallacy as the previous question, hiding at the other end of the proof. [From $u^{2}>1$ you may
conclude $\lvert u\rvert>1$ — and nothing about the sign of $u$]{.hl}. Ask yourself which quadrants have
$\tan\theta>0$ before you decide.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — $u^{2}>1$ gives $\lvert u\rvert>1$, not $u>1$; and the third quadrant is where it bites
:::

**F — the first error is in line (V).**

### Lines (I)–(IV) are all correct

| | | why it holds |
|---|---|---|
| **(I)** | $\sin\theta\cos\theta=\tan\theta\cos^{2}\theta>0$ | $\tan\theta>0$ by assumption and $\cos^{2}\theta>0$ since $\cos\theta\neq0$ ✓ |
| **(II)** | add $1$ to $2\sin\theta\cos\theta>0$ | ✓ |
| **(III)** | replace the leading $1$ by $\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta$ | ✓ an identity |
| **(IV)** | factorise the perfect square | ✓ |

### Why (V) fails

$(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^{2}>1$ gives only

$$\lvert\sin\theta+\cos\theta\rvert>1 ,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \sin\theta+\cos\theta>1 \;\textbf{ or }\; \sin\theta+\cos\theta<-1 .$$

The proof takes the first branch and silently discards the second — and **the second branch is where
$\tan\theta>0$ also lives**.

### The conjecture itself is false

$\tan\theta>0$ in the **first** quadrant *and* in the **third**. Take $\theta=225^\circ$:

$$\tan225^\circ=1>0 ,\qquad \sin225^\circ+\cos225^\circ=-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}=-\sqrt2\approx-1.414 ,$$

which is certainly not greater than $1$. *(And $(-\sqrt2)^{2}=2>1$, so line (IV) is perfectly happy with
this counterexample — the proof survives all the way to the last line before breaking.)*

**The lesson.** [Every time a square disappears, a $\pm$ should appear]{.hl}. Here both branches of
$\lvert u\rvert>1$ are genuinely occupied, so discarding one is not a tidy-up — it is the whole error.
*Compare with [Question 19](#question-19-2021-p2-q5): the same lost sign, once at the start of a chain and once at the
very end.* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 21 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2020 · P2 Q16</span>

::: {.question}
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTC) tells us that for any polynomial $\mathrm{f}$:

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\int_{0}^{x}\mathrm{f}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\right)=\mathrm{f}(x)$$

A student calculates $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\displaystyle\int_{x}^{2x}t^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\right)$ as follows:

> **(I)** &nbsp; $\displaystyle\int_{x}^{2x}t^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{2x}t^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t-\int_{0}^{x}t^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t$
>
> **(II)** &nbsp; By FTC, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x}t^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\right)=x^{2}$
>
> **(III)** &nbsp; By FTC, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2x}t^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\right)=(2x)^{2}=4x^{2}$
>
> **(IV)** &nbsp; So $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\displaystyle\int_{x}^{2x}t^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\right)=4x^{2}-x^{2}$
>
> **(V)** &nbsp; giving $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\displaystyle\int_{x}^{2x}t^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\right)=3x^{2}$

Which of the following best describes the student's calculation?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** completely correct &nbsp;&nbsp;**B** first error on (I) &nbsp;&nbsp;**C** … (II)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** … (III) &nbsp;&nbsp;**E** … (IV) &nbsp;&nbsp;**F** … (V)
:::

The theorem is printed for you, with its upper limit written as **$x$**. [Check each use against the
statement as given, letter by letter]{.hl} — one of the two applications has an upper limit that is not
$x$. You can also settle the whole thing by integrating directly, since $t^{2}$ is easy.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — a theorem applied outside the form in which it is stated; the missing chain rule
:::

**D — the first error is on line (III).**

### Line (II) is a legitimate use; line (III) is not

The FTC as printed has upper limit exactly $x$. Line (II) matches it and is correct. Line (III) has upper
limit $2x$, which the printed statement says nothing about. Doing it properly, with $F(u)=\int_0^u
t^2\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $u=2x$, the chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}F(2x)=F'(2x)\times\frac{\mathrm{d}(2x)}{\mathrm{d}x}=(2x)^{2}\times2=8x^{2},$$

not $4x^{2}$. *The student took the theorem's conclusion and substituted $2x$ for $x$ in it, which is not
what the theorem permits — the factor $2$ from differentiating the limit is lost.*

### The direct check

$$\int_{x}^{2x}t^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t=\left[\frac{t^{3}}{3}\right]_{x}^{2x}=\frac{8x^{3}-x^{3}}{3}=\frac{7x^{3}}{3}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\frac{7x^{3}}{3}\right)=7x^{2} .$$

The correct answer is $7x^{2}$; with line (III) repaired the student's own route gives $8x^{2}-x^{2}=7x^{2}$
too. ✓ *Lines (I), (IV) and (V) are all sound — (I) is the standard splitting of an integral, and (IV) and
(V) simply carry forward the wrong number from (III).*

**The lesson.** [A theorem licenses exactly the statement it makes, and no substitution into its
conclusion]{.hl}. Whenever a variable limit is anything other than a bare $x$, a chain-rule factor is due.
*And when the integrand is simple, compute the thing directly — thirty seconds of honest integration
identifies the wrong line without any theory at all.* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 22 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P2 Q11</span>

::: {.question}
A student attempts to solve the following problem, where $a$ and $b$ are non-zero real numbers:

> Show that **if** $a^{2}-4b^{3}\ge0$ **then** there exist real numbers $x$ and $y$ such that
> $a=xy(x+y)$ and $b=xy$.

Consider the following attempt:

> **(I)** &nbsp; $(x-y)^{2}\ge0$
>
> **(II)** &nbsp; so $x^{2}+y^{2}-2xy\ge0$
>
> **(III)** &nbsp; so $(x+y)^{2}-4xy\ge0$
>
> **(IV)** &nbsp; so $x^{2}y^{2}(x+y)^{2}-4x^{3}y^{3}\ge0$
>
> **(V)** &nbsp; so $a^{2}-4b^{3}\ge0$

Which of the following best describes this attempt?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** It is completely correct.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** It is incorrect, but it would be correct if written in the reverse order.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** It is incorrect, but the student has correctly proved the **converse**.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** incorrect — error in line (II). &nbsp;&nbsp;**E** … (III). &nbsp;&nbsp;**F** … (IV).
:::

Every line here is algebraically true. So before hunting for a slip, [write down what was **asked** and
what was **proved**, as two arrows]{.hl} — the fault in this question is not in any line but in the
direction of the whole thing.

Note also that option **B** is a genuine possibility in general: some chains really can be reversed.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — proving the converse; and why "just reverse it" is not a repair
:::

**C — the student has correctly proved the converse.**

### The algebra is flawless

| | | check |
|---|---|---|
| **(I)→(II)** | expand the square | ✓ |
| **(II)→(III)** | $x^{2}+y^{2}-2xy=(x+y)^{2}-4xy$ | ✓ an identity, since $(x+y)^{2}=x^{2}+2xy+y^{2}$ |
| **(III)→(IV)** | multiply by $x^{2}y^{2}\ge0$ | ✓ multiplying an inequality by a non-negative number is safe |
| **(IV)→(V)** | substitute $a=xy(x+y)$ and $b=xy$ | ✓ $a^{2}=x^{2}y^{2}(x+y)^{2}$ and $4b^{3}=4x^{3}y^{3}$ |

*So there is no line to accuse — which is why D, E and F are wrong.*

### What was actually proved

$$\textbf{Asked: }\quad a^{2}-4b^{3}\ge0\;\Longrightarrow\;\exists\,x,y \text{ with } a=xy(x+y),\ b=xy$$
$$\textbf{Proved: }\quad \exists\,x,y \text{ with } a=xy(x+y),\ b=xy\;\Longrightarrow\;a^{2}-4b^{3}\ge0$$

The attempt **starts** by assuming such $x$ and $y$ exist — they appear in line (I) out of nowhere — and
**ends** at the inequality. That is the converse, and it is correctly established. **C.**

### Why B is wrong

*Reversing the lines would not repair it.* The chain would have to begin at $a^{2}-4b^{3}\ge0$, where no
$x$ and $y$ are available yet, and conclude that suitable ones exist. Each line uses $x$ and $y$, so running
the same lines upwards never produces them. Reversing the algebra is not the obstacle (since $b=xy\neq0$, the
step (III)$\to$(IV) can be undone); the missing piece is the proof that $x$ and $y$ **exist**.

**The lesson.** [When every line checks out and the proof is still wrong, compare the first line with the
hypothesis]{.hl}. A proof that begins by assuming the conclusion — here, the existence of $x$ and $y$ — is
proving the converse, whatever it ends with. *This is the single most valuable habit on the page: read the
first and last lines before reading any of the middle.* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 23 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2022 · P2 Q17</span>

::: {.question}
A student answered the following question:

> $a$ and $b$ are non-zero real numbers. Prove that the equation $x^{3}+ax^{2}+b=0$ has three distinct real
> roots if $\;27b\left(b+\dfrac{4a^{3}}{27}\right)<0$.

Here is the student's solution:

> **I** &nbsp; We differentiate $y=x^{3}+ax^{2}+b$ to get $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=3x^{2}+2ax=x(3x+2a)$.
> Solving $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=0$ shows that the stationary points are at $(0,b)$ and
> $\left(-\dfrac{2a}{3},\;b+\dfrac{4a^{3}}{27}\right)$.
>
> **II** &nbsp; If $27b\left(b+\dfrac{4a^{3}}{27}\right)<0$, then $b$ and $b+\dfrac{4a^{3}}{27}$ must have
> opposite signs, and so one of the stationary points is above the $x$-axis and one is below.
>
> **III** &nbsp; If the cubic has three distinct real roots, then one of the stationary points is above the
> $x$-axis and one is below.
>
> **IV** &nbsp; Hence if $27b\left(b+\dfrac{4a^{3}}{27}\right)<0$, then the equation has three distinct real roots.

Which one of the following options best describes the student's solution?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** It is a completely correct solution.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** The student has instead proved the converse of the statement in the question.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** The solution is wrong, because the student should have stated step II after step III.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** The solution is wrong, because the student should have shown the converse of the result in step II.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** The solution is wrong, because the student should have shown the converse of the result in step III.
:::

The hardest question on the page, and worth the time. [Write each numbered step as an arrow, then see
whether the arrows link up to give the arrow the question asked for]{.hl}. One of them points the wrong
way — and the answer options distinguish very carefully between *the whole statement's converse* and *one
step's converse*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — a chain that does not connect; the converse of an intermediate step, not of the theorem
:::

**E — the student should have shown the converse of the result in step III.**

### Write the steps as arrows

Let $C$ be the condition $27b\left(b+\tfrac{4a^{3}}{27}\right)<0$, let $S$ be *"one stationary point above
the $x$-axis and one below"*, and let $R$ be *"three distinct real roots"*.

$$\textbf{II:}\quad C\Rightarrow S \qquad\qquad \textbf{III:}\quad R\Rightarrow S \qquad\qquad
\textbf{Wanted:}\quad C\Rightarrow R$$

From $C\Rightarrow S$ and $R\Rightarrow S$ nothing follows about $C\Rightarrow R$. *Both arrows point **into**
$S$; to chain them you need one arrow out of it.* The step that is needed is $S\Rightarrow R$ — which is the
**converse of step III**. Hence **E**.

### Step I and step II are correct

Step I: $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=3x^{2}+2ax=x(3x+2a)=0$ at $x=0$ and $x=-\tfrac{2a}{3}$, with

$$y(0)=b ,\qquad y\!\left(-\tfrac{2a}{3}\right)=-\tfrac{8a^{3}}{27}+\tfrac{4a^{3}}{9}+b=b+\tfrac{4a^{3}}{27} . \checkmark$$

Step II: since $27>0$, the condition $27b\left(b+\tfrac{4a^{3}}{27}\right)<0$ says exactly that the
**product of the two stationary values is negative**, so they have opposite signs. ✓ *(Expanding,
$27b^{2}+4a^{3}b$, which is $27\times$ the product of the two stationary values.)*

### Why the other options fail

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | "completely correct" | the arrows do not connect, as above |
| **B** | "proved the converse of the statement" | that would mean proving $R\Rightarrow C$. The student did not: step III gives $R\Rightarrow S$, and step II gives $C\Rightarrow S$ — *neither of those is $R\Rightarrow C$.* |
| **C** | "should have stated II after III" | reordering two correct statements changes nothing; the missing arrow is still missing |
| **D** | "converse of step II" | that would be $S\Rightarrow C$, which is not what is needed either — and in fact step II is already used in the right direction |

*Option B is the trap: "the converse" is in the air, but it is the converse of a **step**, not of the
theorem.*

**The lesson.** [Draw the arrows before judging a multi-step proof]{.hl}. A proof fails to connect whenever
two steps point into the same middle statement, and the repair is always to turn one of them round. *Note
how precise the exam is being here: three of the five options are about converses, and they differ only in
**whose** converse.* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

**The whole session in one line:**

> **Read line by line and stop at the first step that does not follow for every allowed case: divide (by
> zero?), square or root (sign or extra root?), converse (proved?), conclusion (assumed?). Sometimes the honest
> answer is "no error".**
